Female newborn pups of Thyroptera tricolor emerge with a wet weight at birth of 1.3 grams [Wwb = 1.3 grams], a minimal mass that underscores the altricial state of the offspring at parturition. This initial body size is remarkably low even among small-bodied vespertilionoid bats, reflecting an energetic strategy that prioritizes rapid postnatal development over substantial pre-natal investment. Under the stable thermal conditions of the roost, typically maintained around 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the gestation period extends for 110 days [tg = 110 days], equivalent to approximately 3.5 months. This relatively prolonged gestation for a bat of such diminutive proportions likely facilitates a degree of organogenesis that partly compensates for the neonate's low birth mass. The species is strictly monovular, with females consistently producing a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and the annual reproductive output is correspondingly constrained, as a female can produce only about one litter each year [F_R_i = about one litter each year] under the moderate climatic conditions of its Neotropical range.

The ultimate wet weight for adult females is recorded at 4 grams [Wwi = 4 grams], an asymptotic mass that is typical for members of the genus Thyroptera and that represents a roughly three-fold increase over the neonatal weight. This modest adult body size imposes tight constraints on the species' life-history schedule. The time since birth at weaning for the young is 120 days [tx = 120 days] within the same thermal regime of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], a developmental interval that encompasses the suckling juvenile stage and the subsequent dietary transition to solid food. The nursing offspring depend entirely on maternal milk during the initial weeks, and the prolonged weaning period relative to the gestation length suggests that milk provisioning constitutes a substantial energetic burden for the lactating female. Field observations indicate that juveniles continue to roost with their mothers for several weeks after achieving nutritional independence, gradually acquiring the foraging skills necessary for sustained flight and insect capture in the understory of lowland rainforests.

The delay before first reproduction is substantial for a mammal of this body size. Females do not produce their first litter until 621 days after birth [tp = 621 days after birth], living under the same thermal conditions of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] that characterize the roost environment throughout development. This protracted interval to first reproduction is unusual for a bat weighing only 4 grams as an adult, and it implies an extended period of somatic growth and behavioral maturation before reproductive effort begins. The attainment of first litter at this age suggests that Thyroptera tricolor follows a relatively slow pace-of-life syndrome, trading early reproductive output for increased adult survival and perhaps enhanced competitive ability in securing high-quality roosting sites within the rolled leaves of Heliconia and Calathea plants. Comparative data from congeners are sparse, but the available records indicate that this species matures later than many gleaning insectivores of similar mass in the Neotropics.

Longevity records for Thyroptera tricolor indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 12,045 days [am = approximately 12,045 days] under the favorable thermal conditions of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] experienced inside its roosts. This translates to roughly 33 years, an exceptionally extended lifespan for a bat of only 4 grams adult body mass. Such longevity is at the upper end of the distribution for similarly sized Chiroptera and aligns more closely with the survival schedules of larger, slower-living species from temperate regions. The extended lifespan is likely facilitated by the low extrinsic mortality associated with roosting inside tightly furled leaves, which provides substantial protection from predators and from extreme weather fluctuations. The combination of a very late age at first reproduction, a single offspring per year, and extreme longevity positions this species as a classic example of a slow life-history strategy within the bat fauna of Central and South America.

The overall life-history profile of Thyroptera tricolor — exceptionally low fecundity, extreme longevity, and delayed maturation — aligns with predictions from demographic theory for a small mammal that experiences predictably low adult mortality in its specialized roosting niche.
